letterboxd-review-1543318328.title: Tumbbad
letterboxd-review-1543318328.review:
that opening sequence with the grandmother, the nails in the mouth, the sound design, the makeup… genuinely terrifying. and just the general atmosphere of the beginning, with the mother and brother. their costume, their look. proper immersion into a world

then we jump forward in time, and it becomes a little less interesting. although that moment with the grandmother as a tree is super cool. again, wonderful sfx makeup and a real understanding of how to create horror through imagery and mood.

and that’s really where the film shines. every sequence involving hastar when we descend into the belly of the goddess, is just so effective, and exciting, and terrifying. the red, the creature design, the visual effects… top notch.

unfortunately, everything outside of that is considerably less compelling. the domestic storyline with the wife and the family is rather forgettable, and while the relationship between the father and son has some interesting moments, i don’t think it’s explored nearly enough. the commentary on greed is also too on the nose for me to gain any real insights.

so it’s a bit of a hit or miss. the opening had me thinking the film was going to sustain that level of horror throughout, but it never quite does. still, whenever it returns to hastar and that wonderfully disturbing mythology, I was on the edge of my seat.

letterboxd-review-1543120204.title: RRR
letterboxd-review-1543120204.review:
well, it was bound to happen eventually... Rajamouli can’t just make masterpieces, can he

all jokes aside, this is interesting because the signature is clearly there. you can immediately recognize the filmmaker that made Baahubali, but i found this one considerably more uneven in its execution.

i think part of the problem is that Rajamouli feels way more restrained here. Baahubali is completely insane from beginning to end, and you just buy into the world. whereas here, the best moments are precisely those when Rajamouli goes completely unhinged. that sequence with the animals storming the British party for example, is the perfect example, and it’s where his mastery really comes through.
and there are a few other moments like that throughout (like the wonderful dance sequence), but i didn’t feel he was operating at that level consistently.

the friendship between the two protagonists worked overall, although i wouldn’t say i loved it. i liked the way they meet, and i was particularly interested in hot mamdani’s position within the british police. there were Indians who served the colonial authorities during the occupation, and i thought it would have been interesting to explore that contradiction a little more deeply. so when we discover that his loyalty to the british was essentially a ploy from the beginning, i was a little disappointed. however that storyline eventually grew on me, and the flashback with his father was very good, but i still think the original premise could have led somewhere more interesting.

there’s a few things I didn’t buy at all. for example I didn’t buy for a second that the british girl would be interested in the main character which kinda killed the immersion at the beginning.

the way the british villains were portrayed was also interesting... their exaggerated, almost cartoonishly evil characterization is perfectly fine. we’ve seen that kind of villainy in the indiana jones films, and it works within that type of storytelling. but Rajamouli takes it one step further by casting the worst actors in the world to play them; having them all perform as though they’ve never acted before in their lives.
and on paper, i actually find that interesting. the performances become almost as exaggerated as the characters themselves. but in practice, i found it pretty jarring, especially at first. i eventually got used to it, but i’m still not convinced the execution entirely works.

there are plenty of interesting ideas throughout, but not all of them feel fully accomplished.

the storyline involving the little girl is nice, although ultimately forgettable. i did really like the moment when the main character discovers the truth about hot mamdani, through his wife. that was a standout moment.

the action sequences are in general pretty great. we know now that Rajamouli really has an understanding for that type of visual spectacle.

overall, i found the storytelling considerably weaker than in Baahubali, and i simply bought into this world a lot less.
i’m actually glad i watched Baahubali before this as I would have probably disliked RRR even more. having become more familiar with his cinematic language, i can better appreciate what he’s attempting to do, even when i don’t think the execution entirely succeeds.

so yeah, not terrible by any means. some cool moments, some touching moments. but ultimately forgettable.

letterboxd-review-1542369968.title: Bāhubali 2: The Conclusion
letterboxd-review-1542369968.review:
just as good as part 1. you guys tend to think it’s better, but I wouldn’t say so because even though the highs are higher in this one, it’s also more uneven than part 1, especially toward the end.

my biggest issue is probably the pacing of the finale. only a confident genius like Rajamouli would take 2h10 minutes of his 2h40 run time to do a set up and only leaving 30 minutes for the final confrontation. I admire the move and the risk, and for the most part it pays off. but it also puts him at a structural disadvantage.
the final battle feels slightly emotionally rushed, especially the very ending when he ascends the throne.

unfortunately, Baahubali Junior’s girlfriend doesn’t get to be a character. she was beginning to become one in part 1, but she’s given nothing to do in this part. and considering how much this draws from the lion king and the prince of egypt, it’s a shame, because even Nala had more of a presence and personality than she does.

but the absolute highlight of this film is the first two hours, and more specifically, Devasena! her love story with Baahubali Senior is just perfect.

that whole sequence in the palace where Baahubali pretends to be a commoner, like a reversed Aladdin, is too good. the way they look at each other when he finally reveals himself, the way he shows her how to put three arrows on her bow… I can’t… Mr. Rajamouli UNDERSTANDS romance!
also the creativity of that sequence with the bulls with the flaming horns charging the bandits…

and then we get into all the palace politics, the betrayals. obviously, there’s absolutely no subtext in any of this. everything is text. everything is maximalist. but again, it’s done with such honesty! such confidence!
so much so that by the time we reach that incredible sequence with Kattappa’s betrayal, i was almost emotionally overwhelmed.

the whole battle on pride rock, with Baahubali Senior using that enormous tree to block the enemies, timing everything perfectly with the lightning strike haha and setting the tree on fire while he barely flinches. that’s a work of art!
the type of imagination the current MCU wishes it had.

and then the queen mother presenting the baby to the crowd. everyone crying. the betrayal. the cut back to the present with Baahubali Junior falling to his knees before his mother, finally understanding everything. and right after, the extreme close up on the eyes of rage and revenge.

in tears! genuinely in tears.

goosebumps in part 1, tears in part 2. but after this  whole 20 minute sequence of brilliance, it loses a bit of its momentum.

the final battle is still very good, even though i preferred the one in part 1. and it’s funny because for example, the palm trees being pulled back to launch soldiers over the castle walls, i’d seen that sequence before. out of context on youtube. just like the enormous flaming drapes used during the battle in the first film, and obviously they looked completely ridiculous. but within the world established, they completely work.

i do wish the final confrontation with the evil uncle had been a little more emotionally satisfying.
after spending so much time building everything up, the ending deserved a little more room to breathe.

and then all the prince of egypt references, with him leaving the palace and becoming one with the people... top. the music overall is also awesome, in both parts.

why doesn’t Rajamouli have his star on hollywood boulevard I wonder…

letterboxd-review-1541477317.title: Bāhubali: The Beginning
letterboxd-review-1541477317.review:
there’s an old saying that says that if you buy the premise, you buy the bit.

just like John Woo films, at no point does this film pretend to be anything other than what it is: a completely ridiculous, unapologetically over the top epic! and for the most part, it works. Rajamouli seems to be a master of the ridiculous, and yet underneath lies real genuineness for the story and characters.

this felt like watching pure mythology. and it was awesome! goosebumps were had, and not just once. was i completely immersed throughout, no. but more often than not, yes.

the love story turning into a music video? haha why not!

and that’s the thing. in this kind of film, i don’t want realism. i don’t care about realistic makeup, grounded action, restrained performances. on the very contrary. that’s not what the film is trying to accomplish. and that’s precisely why I think something like drishyam or vada dhennai didn’t work. those films have the ambition to tell serious, grounded stories, and i thought they largely failed at what they set out to do. Baahubali, on the other hand, knows exactly what it wants to be, and master Rajamouli delivers (for the most part)

and that final battle… worthy of helm’s deep! what are we even talking about. it was awesome.

bad CGI? who gives a shit. it fits perfectly in this world. I’d be actually concerned if the CGI had been polished.

just a really fun ride, deeply embedded in a culture i’m more than happy to discover.

BAAHUBALI! BAAHUBALI! BAAHUBALI!

can’t wait for part 2

letterboxd-review-1540088625.title: Mayabazar
letterboxd-review-1540088625.review:
what a pleasant surprise…

I knew going into this that it drew from one of india’s great epics, and that there was a considerable amount of mythology behind it. I read a little about it beforehand, although of course not enough to understand every relationship and reference.
but ultimately, the story itself is fairly accessible. two young people fall in love, one family wants to take over the other, and a marriage that was once perfectly acceptable becomes undesirable.
familiar mythological story but it’s not the plot was that particularly fascinated me.

what enchanted me was the sheer whimsical nature of the whole thing. the tone, the atmosphere, the world that the film creates. and i’m actually really glad i watched the colorized version, because the colors are quite sublime. there’s something about that palette, combined with the elaborate sets, and the matte paintings that reminded me of the work of the archers (powell and pressburger), especially black narcissus, or even the grand productions of griffith like intolerance. there’s an artisanal quality to it all.

i was also surprisingly into the love story, especially during the first act, and even more so of the musical sequences. I have been very neutral about the indian musical sequences in general but here, I think they contributed really well to that sense of enchantment.

I do think the film exhausts itself somewhat in the second half: when ghatotkacha enters the story and the narrative becomes largely concerned with his tricks to sabotage the arranged marriage and reunite the lovers. i still enjoyed the visuals, especially the special effects and all the in-camera trickery, which are impressive for the 1950s. there’s some wonderful ingenuity in the way the illusions are accomplished. but narratively, that whole section was a little less compelling.

i’m still somewhat distant from the mythology and from certain aspects of the storytelling of course, but i came away appreciating this far more than i expected it to.

letterboxd-review-1536223096.title: Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma
letterboxd-review-1536223096.review:
i always find myself fascinated by schoenbrun’s work, and especially dumbfounded by how confident they are in their subject matter.
I haven’t seen their first film yet, but i was really impressed by I saw the tv glow, and this only reinforces what i thought.

we often talk about films being personal, but most of the time we use that word a bit loosely. filmmakers have ideas they want to express, stories they want to tell, or just a desire to entertain, and in a way all of that can be personal. but there’s something different here. this film (like their previous one) is about the experience of their identity.

and what they’re attempting to express is what the trans (through little death) and queer (through hannah einbinder) experience feels like to them in all of its facets:  the pain, the joy of discovery, the confusion, living within a society that doesn’t really understand or accept who you are, and all the different emotions that come with that experience.
and they choose to express all of this through some of the most creative filmmaking i’ve seen in recent years.

it’s esoteric, sometimes completely surreal, but there’s always something grounded enough in the emotions that even those of us who could never truly understand what that experience feels like, are allowed to become guests within it.

what makes it even more fascinating is the way they choose to explore these ideas through the slasher genre. the violence and the gore… the very form of the genre become ways of expressing these feelings about identity and repression. it’s fascinating to take a genre that is so often associated with fear and the monstrous and using it to explore what it feels like to be perceived as different.

and the filmmaking itself is quite wonderful as well. the film grain, the production design, especially everything surrounding candy. all these little visual choices that make the world feel like an extension of the character’s internal conflict. there’s a real understanding of how to use the medium to communicate something that would be almost impossible to express through dialogue alone.

there’s also this whole exploration of repressed fantasies and taboos, the things we’re not supposed to say or even allow ourselves to imagine.
there’s a liberation in the form, but also something uncomfortable and almost nightmarish, and the film keeps moving between those feelings with a visual language reminiscent of lynch, de palma, or even carpenter and cronenberg.

and for the most part, it works very well.

however there are moments that don’t quite land emotionally, and especially the ending, which i thought was weaker than what came immediately before it. I think the film could have ended one scene earlier and been much stronger for it.

all in all, there’s a lot to admire here, and what continues to impress me about schoenbrun is how unapologetic they are in their artistic expression. a real understanding of what this art form is capable of.

letterboxd-review-1534522830.title: The Invite
letterboxd-review-1534522830.review:
I mean, we can cut to the chase. yes, this was brilliant.

brilliant in writing, performances, pacing, editing, direction. my goodness, the compositions. the blocking, the staging... we’re talking about someone who truly understands cinema and dramaturgy. who understands when to cut, when to stay on a shot, when to move the camera and why a change in angle matters.

and i really hope those of you who loved this film paid attention to the craft, because it all seems so simple, so easy... it’s essentially four people in one apartment talking to each other, and yet every piece of production design, light choice, every color (or lack thereof), every mannerism, every shot and camera movement is enhancing the storytelling. and that is unusual for this to be done at that level for this type of film. everything works together so seamlessly that it feels effortless.

now, i will say that the first 10 to 15 minutes, before the title card arrives, were a little difficult for me to get into. everything felt a little too rushed. including the jokes, the banter between rogen and wilde that felt a tad caricatural, even the music was so frantic that i felt like the film was overcompensating and wasn’t giving me the space to properly laugh or be properly immersed. it was doing too much, and I actually got scared.

but then the title card arrives, the neighbors come in, and suddenly it all comes into its own.

and from that moment on, the comedy is pretty much perfect. rogen becomes the best actor in the film. the man just proves again (in case we’ve forgotten) that he is a monster at what he does. his comedic timing, his delivery, his face work, the way he can get a laugh out of the smallest reaction. it’s just unbelievable.

and of course, everyone else is brilliant too. the casting is impeccable. and even with veterans of the game like rogen, norton and cruz in front of her, olivia wilde holds her own against all of them no questions asked. she gives a performance with a level of nuance and vulnerability that she’s never shown before.
the improv in general is so strong that you can barely distinguish where the writing ends and the performances begin.

even the music, which bothered me so much at the beginning, becomes incredibly effective throughout the rest of the film. when it comes in, how long it stays, the type of music being used. there’s such an innate understanding of how a score should participate in the storytelling.

and then there’s the writing.

it’s real, it’s heartfelt, it’s genuine, it’s horny and exciting, and there’s so much insight into human relationships and the way people behave when they’re confronted with things they’ve spent years refusing to acknowledge.

and obviously, this movie was practically made for me. I’ve experienced almost all of that. I once was rogen, and norton, and especially cruz lol. the film captures these different facets of human nature with an incredible amount of honesty.

and it’s all there in the writing, but also in the performances. in the way these people speak to each other, the way they walk around the apartment, their demeanor, their little reactions, the things they say and the things they refuse to say. there’s such a genuine understanding of human behavior throughout, and the film manages to be absolutely hilarious while also becoming moving.

and that ending is just sublime.

that final shot, so subtly framed within the window, surrounded by all that black, such restraint… like we’re looking at an old photograph. the film doesn’t have to say anything here, because everything has already been expressed.

for those who loved this, I strongly recommend you watching paul mazursky’s bob & carol & ted & alice from 1969 (with natalie wood), which is the OG, and brilliant as well.
there’s no “the invite” without that film, and it’s fascinating to see how a similar exploration of relationships, sexuality and marriage is approached in two completely different eras.

now, i know you guys are going to ask me whether i prefer this or digger for best film of the year so far, and i genuinely don’t know. i think the highs of digger are higher. it’s more ambitious and takes more risks. but the invite, for what it is is a little jewel.

and I’m actually really glad I didn’t watch this one in theater. it’s such an intimate film. my living room was the perfect setting.

wether it’s best film of the year, or second best, one thing’s for sure,
we now have our second minor masterpiece of 2026.

letterboxd-review-1532691971.title: Tony
letterboxd-review-1532691971.review:
charming little film. nowhere near the praise you guys have been giving it, but decent nonetheless.

it’s a well made, conventional, relatively safe film that does some things really well, but it never quite offers much beyond what you’d expect from this type of story.

what i liked most was the approach to the self discovery, and especially the decision to focus on this very specific period of tony’s life rather than giving us another generic biopic that tries to cover everything from beginning to end. the film captured tony’s coming of age quite genuinely.

a lot of that comes from the editing, which i thought was one of the best aspect of the film. there’s a natural flow to the way we’re immersed in this world. the montage sequences were lovely. the editing allows us to experience the environment alongside tony as he slowly finds his place within it. some memorable characters in that kitchen, some not so much.

and of course, dominic sessa is wonderful. he’s just so believable in everything he does. his posture, his mannerisms, his demeanor, even the smallest reactions feel completely natural. he carries so much of the film simply through the way he inhabits the character.
his chemistry with banderas or the guy from white lotus was great as well.

unfortunately, the romantic storyline is nowhere near as interesting.

the relationship between Tony and the girl feels incredibly generic, almost cookie cutter in the way it’s written. the chemistry isn’t convincing, and the whole situation with her boyfriend, especially how easily that relationship falls apart, is so convenient and unrealistic and you can practically see the screenplay moving things around just to get to the next plot point.

and because the film spends so much time on that relationship (as one always does in a coming of age story), it feels like we’re watching two different movies. they’re obviously both part of tony’s journey of self discovery, but one is so much more interesting and genuine than the other that the imbalance becomes increasingly noticeable.

and that’s really where my main issue with the film lies. even when it works, whether through the filmmaking or the storytelling, it remains so conventional in its approach. the emotional beats are nice, the characters are likable, but there’s very little that feels particularly insightful or memorable beyond the immediate experience of watching it.

even the ending, with tony finally accepting himself and who he is, works well enough. but again, it doesn’t really take the film anywhere beyond what it had already established.

am I going to forget most of this film? most likely. am I being generous with three stars? probably.

but sessa is peak, the editing is wonderful, and there are some genuine moments throughout.

it’s good. it’s nice. it does the job.

letterboxd-review-1530947691.title: Primetime
letterboxd-review-1530947691.review:
first and foremost, anyone who thinks this film is excusing or sympathizing with predators, or that it’s some kind of hit piece on chris hansen, or anything of that nature, you’re officially an idiot and you do not deserve this art form. actually, any art form for that matter. you should probably refrain from consuming art altogether. it’s okay, it doesn’t have to be for everyone. clearly it’s not for you.

so that’s first of all.

now, as for the film itself, the first half was wonderful. visually, structurally, the way we’re immersed into the world and into the mind of hansen, who’s immediately established as multifaceted. and more importantly, the film superbly sets up a premise that was fascinating.

there’s that moment in the NBC offices where hansen is essentially presented with the possibility of becoming the biggest show in the network’s history. and i thought, okay, we’re really going to explore what it means to do the right thing. what happens when someone genuinely believes they’re doing good, but that good is being first pursued for profit, for fame, for ambition, and potentially at the expense of justice itself. what happens when the pursuit of justice becomes entertainment, and what are the consequences of that.

the problem is that the film never really explores it.

there’s sort of an attempt to do so, but it remains far too shallow, and the screenplay never quite knows what to do with the questions it raises. the whole subplot with his mistress and his wife doesn’t really work, and it’s not particularly interesting. and even the final sequence with the predator isn’t nearly enough to make that exploration satisfying.

now, I did still enjoy it. I liked being in hansen’s psyche. but a huge part of that is because pattinson was incredible.
and this is coming from someone who has never been fully sold on pattinson. very good in the lighthouse and the batman, but he’s never particularly blown me away. here, he actually did.

the choices he makes are thoughtful. his mannerisms, his diction, the way he pauses to think about what he’s going to say or do next, and all the little nuances that make you believe in this man who’s genuinely convinced of the importance of his mission, while simultaneously becoming consumed by his own ambition. even as his mental state begins to deteriorate, there’s something very convincing about the way pattinson carries those contradictions.
he takes real risks with the performance, and they work. even when the screenplay isn’t giving him nearly enough to work with.

gisondo is very good too, and merritt wever is fantastic. there’s a lot to appreciate in the performances throughout, which makes the shortcomings of the writing even more frustrating.

visually, the film remains excellent from beginning to end. and that’s also one of the main aspects that kept me engaged till the end.

so i didn’t dislike it. there’s a lot to admire in it.
but unfortunately, it slowly exhausts itself as it goes, and by the end i was left thinking about how much better it could have been. because those first 40 minutes promised something genuinely awesome. a film that was going to dig into all kinds of moral contradictions.

alas, primetime doesn’t live up to its own premise.

letterboxd-review-1524287017.title: Bramayugam
letterboxd-review-1524287017.review:
This review may contain spoilers.

this is every bit as good as the lighthouse.

obviously there’s the idea of power corrupting, and absolute power corrupting absolutely, which runs through the entire thing, but what kept catching my eye is the masterful exercise in style and atmosphere. the way the film slowly takes you deeper into the nightmare. a journey through hell, except the hell is as much inside these characters minds as it is the actual place.

you can feel the sweat and the dread. the cinematography to the production design was on point; bleak and anxiety-inducing. even the opening was reminiscent of the game of thrones prologue.

the performances are overall great. especially Mammootty. his presence is adequately unsettling, and when we finally get to the goblin coming out of his body, the design is superb. the textures, the face, the way it looks and moves. striking imagery, and incredible makeup work.

I also really liked seeing the portuguese soldiers at the end. after spending the entire film trapped in this house, suddenly the world opens up again, except now the colonizers are coming. it makes everything we’ve just watched feel like part of something much larger and uncertain.

I’m not sure it needed to be 2h20. but for most of its runtime, the film is quite effective.

letterboxd-review-1520647337.title: Digger
letterboxd-review-1520647337.review:
first things first, the marketing team behind this and whoever created those trailers should all be fired, effective immediately.

now that that’s out of the way, ladies and gentlemen, we finally have the first minor masterpiece of the year. (I say this having not seen the invite yet)

it’s not perfect, and there are things I wanted more from, but overall this is brilliant. as a piece of satire, as a commentary, as a piece of art. it’s mature, intelligent, thought-provoking, emotional, hilarious, and manages to excel at the layers it keeps revealing along the way.

yes, Tom Cruise is impeccable. his best and most nuanced performance for sure. i had serious doubts after the trailers because i thought he was going to be way too over the top, but once you actually see the film, you understand why the performance is what it is. there are layers to what he’s doing that i would love to get into, but i genuinely can’t without ruining part of the experience.

and that’s actually the problem i’m having writing this review. i can barely talk about the film, because talking about it would immediately spoil it.

something happens that completely changes your perspective on what you’ve been watching. it changes the commentary, it reinvents the genre, and suddenly the structure itself becomes part of what the film is saying. i don’t even want to hint at what that means because you really should go into this blind. once you see it, you’ll understand why i’m being so vague and why it’s annoying me so much.

what i can talk about is what’s on the surface, and even there, this thing is firing on pretty much every cylinder.

right from the first three succession of shots, you know a master is speaking. but really, the whole thing is masterful. there’s such an economy to the shots, and such confidence in the blocking. something as simple as a character opening a door and momentarily hiding someone else in the frame… everything is minutely thought out. the production design, the costumes, the sound design… (especially the sound design!)
seeing that level of command over the craft is becoming increasingly rare and it’s truly a breath of fresh air.

and then there’s the monologue everybody is talking about. cruise is unbelievable, but the scene works this well because everything around him is operating at the same level. the direction, the camera work, the color palette of the room, the costumes of the extras, the editing, the performances. even the desaturated grading that I hated in the trailers ended up being one of the best part of the film because, again, there’s a reason for it that i cannot talk about.

but most importantly, the spectacular writing. the writing is excellent throughout, but stands out the most in that scene. it’s real and metaphorical. heartfelt and powerful while avoiding the generic cliches these types of monologues usually run into.

the whole scene is a painting. one of the best scenes of the year and probably one of the best scenes of the century.

the performances across the board are stellar. John Goodman, Riz Ahmed, even the secondary characters (especially the dad from gossip girl). the dramatic and comedic timing is overall impeccable, which is especially important because this is a film that speaks a lot. the excellent screenplay and the sharp dialogue are doing a lot of the work.
and it ends also perfectly. even the color of the font of the end credits is correct.

all that being said, there are things that don’t work quite as well. i wanted more from cruise and his daughter and that entire plot line. there are weaker characters (sandra huller), and i think there are places where the film could have gone slightly deeper emotionally.
I also didn’t have that overwhelming visceral reaction at the end that would push this into the very highest level for me. but these are details within something that is quite extraordinary.

go in blind. as blind as you can.

for now (from everything i’ve seen this year), this is easily the best film of 2026.

the haters have no idea what they’re talking about. and they can suck it.

letterboxd-review-1519011129.title: Hope
letterboxd-review-1519011129.review:
is it ridiculous? of course. but it completely owns how ridiculous it is. to the point where you can’t help but really enjoy it.

at some point, any suspension of disbelief just goes out the window and it just becomes hilarious. but I really think that’s the point. na hong-jin is a master and I think he knows exactly the kind of film he’s making.
the wailing and chaser were obviously much more serious films but still, he dabbled with the absurd. (especially in the wailing).
here he decides to swing into the territory of sci-fi, fantasy, action, comedy, all at once. and somehow it works a lot of the time.

sometimes it doesn’t. there are definitely moments where it pushes it too far, and some of the fights become so random and overly long that they took me out. for example the fight in the woods with michael fassbender went on for way too long, while the whole sequence with the car and the horse was nonsensically awesome.

but what i really loved was the mythology around all of it. the spaceship, the hunters going inside and exploring it, the design of everything, all the little details and easter eggs that make you feel like there’s an entire world here beyond what we’re seeing. even the exposition with the aliens at the end is so random and weird and awesome. I applaud this type of absurd world building.

the production design is incredible too. the sets are wonderful, the slow motion is effective, and even the CGI, which was questionable at the beginning, eventually becomes better and better. there’s something about the artificiality of the whole thing that feels completely intentional. almost like he’s playing with the language of the action genre itself and through his style, constantly commenting on it.

it’s fun and cool and I really didn’t expect it to take this many swings. not all of them land, but when they do, they really do.

letterboxd-review-1518270326.title: Kumbalangi Nights
letterboxd-review-1518270326.review:
there’s one sequence in this film that i really really loved. and I think it will stick with me.

first of all, the way grief was explored through the older brother’s character was very special.
and the sequence I’m talking about is the one in the midpoint. when he’s almost committing suicide, his friend trying to save him, the discovery of the body, the lamp dangling back and forth. watching that, I was like, okay the film begins.

and everything that immediately follows with him is just as good. he’s a great actor, and there’s something real about the way he carries that grief. the moments where he just stares into the void, or when he finally breaks down crying in his friend’s arms. you can feel the loss of his father, all this pain that has been sitting inside of him for so long.

and then you have that juxtaposed with the younger brother and the girl, and for a little while the film becomes genuinely poetic. the music is great, the young brother’s performance is finally convincing, editing and structure suddenly come together quite beautifully. ngl I teared up a little.

unfortunately, the rest doesn’t hold up.

it’s too uneven, and for the most part, just very ordinary. the filmmaking is generic but does the job. it’s not particularly good or bad, it’s good enough, but there’s very little directorial or artistic point of view behind anything.

the relationships are hit or miss too. the relationship between the younger brother and the girl is interesting, but never becomes anything particularly special, probably because it’s lacking chemistry. the mute brother and the american girl was pretty weak, and the older brother with the widow felt too abrupt.

there are also ideas that are introduced without ever being properly explored. the creepy behavior from the protagonist at the cinema for example, is interesting, but i never really understood what the filmmaker wanted to do with it.
character nuances in general are not well explored unfortunately.
and the overall relationship between all the brothers is nice, but because most of it is surface level, it does not land as well as it intends.

and then the horror action film at the end haha, I mean why not. the guy standing silently in the corner for 15 minutes is ridiculous but also pretty funny, and tbh i had fun with the ending for what it was.

i just kept wishing there was more of what i saw in that section about grief. because for those few scenes, everything clicked and there was something genuinely beautiful there.

the rest is just too subpar.

letterboxd-review-1512820413.title: Super Deluxe
letterboxd-review-1512820413.review:
first of all, I hope you guys can see the difference between the film i watched yesterday (not cinema), and this (cinema).

the difference is night and day.

and talking about cinema, the filmmaking here is astounding:
cinematography. color grading. compositions. camera movement. all of it impeccable.

and on top of that, SPECTACULAR blocking!

the shots are not just well composed, they’re highly creative.

always something happening visually. foregrounds. middle grounds. backgrounds!
characters doing things in the background that have absolutely nothing to do with drawing attention to themselves but make the entire world feel real and alive.

no extra is just randomly standing somewhere because the director needed somebody to fill the screen.
everybody has something to do. everyone has a personality.

also contrary to yesterday’s film, this filmmaker embraces patience. there are shots that last forever allowing us to absorb all the needed information and emotion.
the filmmaker doesn’t panic and cut because he thinks we’re going to get bored. he understands that if the blocking is good enough and what is happening inside the frame is compelling enough, you will be mesmerized by it.

and for most of the time, he succeeds.

the compositions are constantly playing with frames within frames, depth, movement, geometry. even when the filmmaking suddenly goes from static to handheld, it feels completely intentional.

and then there’s the color.

this filmmaker has enormous taste.

the saturation is perfect. the costumes, production design, cinematography and color grading all work in complete symbiosis. colors are constantly complementing or contrasting each other without ever feeling like someone just discovered a color wheel.

that first sequence alone, when the camera leaves the woman and the man having sex and starts moving around the room.

you immediately know you’re in good hands.

and to be clear, this isn’t about every movie needing to look like super deluxe. obviously not. vada chennai is attempting a completely different style.
the problem is that it fails at the style it’s attempting.

super deluxe is pristine visual storytelling. filmmaking that understands exactly where to put the camera, when to move it, when not to move it, when to cut and, more importantly, when to just wait.

and that level of filmmaking allows for some really compelling narrative sequences.

the hospital oner with the mother pleading for someone to save her son is phenomenal.

she’s breaking down in the foreground, desperately trying to save her child. in the middle ground, people are watching this woman completely fall apart. and in the background, the cleaning women are just sweeping the floor.

life continues. but for her, the entire universe is collapsing. and for everybody else, it’s another day at the hospital.

that’s blocking. that’s filmmaking. that’s using every layer of the frame to tell the story instead of simply pointing the camera at the person speaking.

wonderful sequence.

the police-station sequence with shilpa is incredible too. honestly, almost everything involving shilpa and her son was great. that entire storyline is probably the strongest of the film. the performance is fantastic, the relationship with the kid works, and the way that storyline ultimately resolves is emotionally cathartic.
(however i could have used more of the mother and that family dynamic)

the sequence where the other kid discovers his mother in the porn film, completely loses his mind, runs toward her with intent to kill and ends up impaling himself is also one of the highlights.

then you have the couple trying to get rid of the body, which has some engaging and funny moments throughout. but not as good as the previous segment talked about. however I loved when the television falls on the corrupt cop. beautifully random

because randomness is obviously one of the major ideas running through this entire thing. destiny, coincidence, absurdity…

and that’s where the pulp fiction and especially magnolia references come in.

the problem is that those storylines aren’t equally compelling narratively speaking.

pulp fiction is considerably more consistent from story to story in terms of interest and pacing, and magnolia is basically perfect at it.

super deluxe is much more uneven.

there’s also something slightly off about the distribution and pacing of the different narratives, even though the film as a whole mostly moves pretty well.

the storyline with the group of friends is definitely the weakest for me.
the part of the alien. I didn’t dislike it. i actually had fun with it. but it feels like it arrives from a slightly different movie.

and again, magnolia does something similar with the frogs, but by the time the frogs fall from the sky, the movie has already established a world where something like that somehow feels possible. there are anomalies running throughout it. even something like everybody suddenly singing the same song has already pushed the film outside straightforward reality.

so when the impossible happens, i buy it.

super deluxe, despite the incredibly heightened colors and all the absurdity of what happens, actually feels fairly grounded for most of its runtime.

so the alien is a fun idea but kind of comes out of nowhere. it needed to be integrated into the language of the film a little better.

and that’s probably my biggest issue with the movie in general. even tonally, it wasn’t always consistent.

also not a huge fan of the ending.
it becomes a little too preachy. a little too interested in explaining what all this randomness and interconnectedness means.

we didn’t need that. the alien can exist. the television can randomly fall. the mother can have that conversation with her son in the hospital. these people’s lives can collide in completely absurd ways.

that’s enough. you don’t need to explain the universe to me afterward.

that’s another reason something like magnolia works so well. the randomness is allowed to remain random. the film doesn’t need to sit me down afterward and explain why frogs fell from the sky.

I don’t really know how much of super deluxe i’m going to actually remember besides the filmmaking. but what I do know now, is when the narrative worked, I loved it.

and even when the narrative wasn’t completely working, I was fascinated in watching pure cinema.

letterboxd-review-1510862233.title: Vada Chennai
letterboxd-review-1510862233.review:
the one thing I appreciated here is getting to learn about the culture and its political history

north chennai has this fascinating specific working-class history tied to fishing communities and its underworld.

I would have loved to see a filmmaker adapt it.

because guys, let’s be serious here, this is barely a film.

and there’s no language or cultural barrier here. nobody suddenly breaks into a musical number. there isn’t some odd cinematic language that a foreigner would struggle to understand.

this is just awful filmmaking and storytelling on pretty much every level.

the approach to the story is unbelievably uninteresting. not the history, or the true events behind it (that actually sounds fascinating). the actual narrative constructed out of it.

whether it’s the gang politics, anbu slowly getting pulled into this world, or his relationship with the girl, there is just so little here that’s actually compelling from a narrative perspective.

the characters aren’t interesting enough. they’re not developed enough. anbu himself isn’t charismatic enough for me to give a shit about what happens to him.

and the screenplay drags!

there’s such a massive problem with pacing and momentum that the runtime becomes insane. eventually i wasn’t wondering where the story was going. i was wondering when it was going to end.

but somehow the filmmaking might be even worse.

from the first shot, i knew i was in the hands of no one.

this feels like a school project. there is no visual language whatsoever.
it genuinely feels like somebody took a canon 5d, brought a bunch of friends into multiple locations and started randomly filming them. and that could’ve been interesting if that was the intention. but it wasn’t.

which is especially frustrating because some of these locations had a lot of potential.

every shot is poorly composed. poorly blocked. poorly lit. the camera moves are awful. the slow motion is also awful. the cinematography occasionally becomes merely fine and then immediately goes back to looking completely junior.

and the editing!

my god, that was the worst part.

there are cuts every two fucking seconds and half of them feel completely arbitrary. cutting for the sake of cutting. breaking the 180-degree line for absolutely no reason. no visual intention behind the coverage, no intention behind the camera placement or movement, no intention behind the set pieces.

nothing.

and then you have moments where the characters themselves behave in ways that completely destroy the believability of what you’re watching.

there’s an early stabbing where the guy falls onto the horn of a motorcycle and just keeps honking it.
the people who stabbed him are trying not to alert everybody around them.
so naturally, instead of moving his body off the horn, they just leave him there, HONKING.
and then everybody hears it and comes running.

what are we doing hahaha

this is one of many examples. characters aren’t behaving like actual human beings trying to accomplish something. they’re behaving in whatever nonsensical way the screenplay requires in order for the next thing to happen.

and then on top of everything else, it’s just boring.

there was also one thing that I found so bizarre but I know that’s probably not the movie’s fault. it must be mandated by the government.

every time somebody smokes, drinks or does drugs, this little health warning suddenly appears at the bottom of the screen telling you it’s bad for you. they also had blurred nudity as if I was watching a commercial on the bbc

i have never seen that before. insane to mandate that on a narrative film. but again, that’s not the fault of the filmmakers.

nayakan for example is uneven. obviously. there were things in that film that didn’t completely work.
but you can feel a filmmaker behind it with every frame.

this is the opposite. and I feel like I’m being a tad generous with my rating. but the reason why I’m a little generous is because there is one thing that I appreciated:

north chennai.

learning about these communities. the political relationships. the gangs. the fishing communities. the importance they give to the land.

would’ve been better inside a documentary.

anyways, I’m glad we can all welcome together the first dud of the indian cinema journey… 🫡

letterboxd-review-1509649021.title: Nayakan
letterboxd-review-1509649021.review:
Im as surprised as anyone that I actually liked this haha. even really liked it.

even though it’s uneven and we’ve all seen the godfather.

for most of the film, this was a solid 3 stars. but the ending brought it to 3.5.
when the grandkid asks if he’s good or bad, and he says I don’t know… I actually teared up haha. this put everything into perspective. and that actor sold that moment so perfectly. actually, that actor sold every single moment so perfectly.

he’s easily the highlight!

there’s something so subtle and complex and nuanced about what he’s doing, especially with his face work. he never pushes the tragedy of the character onto you. you can just see this man who genuinely wants to do good, who is trying to survive, who believes in what he’s doing, and who also slowly becomes something he himself can’t entirely define.

the aging is really impressive.

obviously the makeup is phenomenal, but it’s not just the makeup. the actor actually changes the way velu exists as he gets older. his mannerisms change. the way he looks at people. the way he speaks. even the way he carries himself changes.

by the time you get to that final scene, i completely believed that I had watched this man live an entire life.

and his relationship with his children, especially his daughter, really works. there’s a genuine sadness there.

the filmmaking is weirdly uneven too, because there are moments that are fairly conventional and then suddenly the cinematography becomes wonderful.

when it’s good, it’s really good.

and i actually really liked the musical sequences here:
the holi sequence especially is one of the best of the whole film. perfectly captured the feeling of an entire community being alive.

and something else i really appreciated was learning about the cultural and political background:
the Tamil migrants living within Bombay, maintaining their own language and identity while existing inside another culture, and the differences in language and dialect that come with that.
the fact that this gangster story is also being used to tell the story of that community made the world considerably more interesting to me.

overall, there’s a genuine heart to the film that kept winning me over even when individual elements didn’t completely work.

good man or bad man?

i don’t know.

👌

letterboxd-review-1507902656.title: Resident Evil
letterboxd-review-1507902656.review:
some of you were wondering, especially when spider-man: brand new day came out, if I still knew how to have fun when watching movies.

and my response was that it was impossible to have fun during most of these films, and especially bnd as it was an awful film from A to Z.

if your characters aren’t interesting, your villain is underwhelming, the writing is sloppy, the world isn’t compelling and if nothing happening on that screen makes you care emotionally or intellectually, then i’m not going to have fun just because the movie tells me i’m supposed to.

ladies and gentlemen, RE is what competent fun looks like.
the perfect example that fun does not come at the expense of good writing or good craft.

RE has great writing. believable dialogue. witty humor. natural banter. no telling, all showing. it respects its audience! trusts them that they can understand something without having it explained to them. creates a world you actually want to be in and most importantly, gives us a character we actually want to follow.

I knew this was going to be special the second bryan hit that first zombie with his car.

because you know exactly what would happen in any other zombie movie. he gets out. slowly approaches the body. gets a little too close. zombie jumps up. jump scare.

instead, he walks over, picks the fucking thing up and puts it in his car.

it’s believable. it’s hilarious. it’s fresh. it’s smart. I’m in.

austin abrams is fantastic because bryan is exactly how we would be in this scenario, or how we would look like playing this game for the first time.

he’s the perfect everyday guy. he isn’t inexplicably great at anything. the way he progresses with the gunplay almost feels like the way we would progress through a difficult shooter. he learns. he adapts. he gets just a little better.

even when he sees those two creatures connecting through their ligaments and basically goes, “that’s interesting.”

yeah. that’s exactly what I would say. it’s not just hilarious, it’s relatable.

and that grounding is so important because it protects the suspension of disbelief. that was one of my biggest problems with barbarian. characters would make decisions that felt so obviously stupid that i stopped believing in the reality of what i was watching.

RE almost never does that.

and then there’s the way cregger translates the language of video games into cinema.

we’re practically introduced to bryan from behind, following him while he’s making a delivery, like we just picked up the controller in a third-person game.

then throughout the film you have the subtle first-person shooter perspectives. the pans left and right that are timed perfectly. the way bryan moves through spaces. the locks! even those tiny pauses when opening doors that immediately puts us back into the gameplay of the last of us.

the attention to detail is precise and staggering and it’s execution is at times jaw dropping.

cregger clearly understands the medium he’s paying homage to, but he never panders to it. he doesn’t need to rely on the recognizable heroes of the games or constantly point at the source material and wait for us to clap.

he takes the cinematic language that players know instinctively and builds something innately fresh out of it.

the environments are wonderful as well. every new location feels like entering another level of a banger video game.
it has its own visual identity, its own obstacles, its own creatures, and, most importantly, it feels lived in! we constantly have the feeling that something happened there before we arrived.

even the “NPCs” have backstories.
there are photographs on walls. objects in houses. little pieces of production design that tell you who these people were without stopping the movie to explain any of it.

that entire opening with the husband, the wife and the dog is such a great example. all these little details eventually connect, come full circle, and all of it suddenly feels so much bigger than what it appears.

that’s impeccable world-building.

and cregger keeps renewing the film like that till the end.
new environment. new situation. new visual ideas.

the elevator sequence is great. the creature design is fantastic. the jump scares mostly work. the production design is really effective. there are some genuinely great shots. and even some of the stranger details that aren’t completely explained never bothered me because they almost feel like easter eggs. little pieces of this world that maybe mean something, maybe don’t, maybe become clearer the further you dig into it.

exactly like in a video game.

it’s as inventive in its progression as the best games know how to be, which is why it basically never drags.

of course, not every section is equally strong. i liked the maxine sequence, but it was definitely one of the weaker ones. the relationship between bryan and his girlfriend also starts much stronger than it ends, and the voice note toward the end doesn’t fully hit.

there are little lags here and there. moments that could have been better. but that’s really all they are.

and i love the way it ends. reminiscent of the phenomenal ending of cabin in the woods (although this one was not exactly at that level)

there’s also something else that makes me really happy, which is just seeing zach cregger get better.

i’ve always really liked the guy as a human being. i love listening to him in interviews. i love his passion. i love how much he clearly cares about filmmaking and the craft.

but i’ve never fully connected with his films until now. (even though he always takes big swings)

barbarian wasn’t good. weapons was better. and resident evil is even better than weapons.

he just keeps progressing. and that’s really inspiring.

because none of what works feels accidental. you can feel how much thought went into the writing, the environments, the camera moves, the creatures, the jokes, the character behavior, the production design, the tiny fucking pause before somebody walks through a door.

that’s where the fun comes from.

not from lowering your standards because something isn’t trying to be profound.

this has absolutely no pretension to be anything other than what it is.

but it executes the shit out of what it is.
and that’s the difference.

it creates a character i want to follow, puts him in a world i want to explore, respects me enough not to explain every tiny thing, understands the medium it’s borrowing from and then uses actual filmmaking craft to turn all of that into a thrilling experience.

it’s not a masterpiece.

but it’s a really, really, really solid film.

and so much fucking fun!

letterboxd-review-1507106466.title: Pyaasa
letterboxd-review-1507106466.review:
I don’t think I’ve ever encountered this type of cinematic language before. how does one even think of this, let alone do this in 1957!

a genuine culture clash was happening while I was watching. the poetry transforming into song, the dream sequences and the realism, the mix of theatrical sets and real locations. its sincere but also awkward and also serious and also a fairy tale.

did I necessarily love that language? i don’t know. there were definitely moments I loved: almost every moment when Vijay was with the girls, especially the scenes in the staircase. Vijay and his family. Vijay and the homeless man. the riot of the people at the end. the final shot…
other times I felt completely disconnected.

I think I found it more astonishing, than emotional.

it made me think a lot about dostoevsky’s the idiot. someone with such a pure soul being thrown into a world that simply isn’t made for someone like him.

love and artistry vs. wealth and status

and there’s almost a structure similar to ikiru. especially in the third act, and the way the film slowly exposes the hypocrisy of everyone around vijay and the society he lives in.

I’m so glad I watched this. never seen anything quite like it. and I can see how years later, we get to moulin rouge.

fascinating experience.

letterboxd-review-1505850631.title: Interview
letterboxd-review-1505850631.review:
this might be the most stylistically radical film of the indian cinema journey so far.

it’s 1970 and mrinal sen is already breaking the fourth wall haha. playing with reality, using these incredibly aggressive montages, interrupting his own narrative and basically treating the entire film as a formidable exercise in style.

the french new wave influence is all over this. but there’s also something eisensteinian about the editing and the way sen uses the collision of images to communicate political ideas rather than simply having characters explain them.

and it’s very interesting how all of that experimentation is being used to explore the aftermath of british colonialism.

the entire premise is simple. a man needs a western suit for a job interview. but through that, sen explores a society where appearance can become more valuable than ability, and where colonialism may technically be over while its values and hierarchies remain embedded in the culture.

fascinating.

there’s also something very confrontational about the way the film pushes against any romanticized idea of british colonialism. independence didn’t magically erase what came before it. sen is interested in what was left behind. the mentality. the class structures. the poverty. the expectation that success still requires performing an image inherited from the people who once ruled you.

it’s far from perfect, but I really wasn’t expecting something this formally adventurous.

awesome stuff.

letterboxd-review-1502889401.title: The Cloud-Capped Star
letterboxd-review-1502889401.review:
ah, so this is where shameless got it from.

a young woman sacrificing her own happiness to keep an entire ungrateful family afloat while everybody around her happily continues living their lives at her expense. sounds about right.

but I’m not gonna waste your time. let’s get right into the filmmaking!

from the first two frames, you know you’re in the hands of a magician.

the blocking. the deep focus. the use of foregrounds, midgrounds, backgrounds. the way characters move within the frame while the camera moves with them, constantly revealing and reorganizing information without cutting.

this is kurosawa-spielberg level blocking.

the world of apu was already easily the most impressive film of the indian cinema journey so far in terms of blocking, framing, and overall visual language.

this beats it in that department.

there is not a single wasted frame in this film. every composition is doing something. people enter, leave, cross each other, disappear into backgrounds, reappear in foregrounds. ghatak can communicate more information through one carefully constructed shot than most filmmakers could with five different setups.

and it’s not just the blocking. the editing is incredibly expressive. the sudden cuts away from the characters to landscapes and environments, the way images collide with each other, the use of sound. the lighting, especially during the night interiors. the sequences involving music. the scenes with the mother.

sublime.

and coming directly from satyajit ray makes the difference in temperament even more fascinating.

ray is quiet. patient. observational. he waits.

ritwik is unbelievably dynamic.

the dialogue is snappy, the banter feels like everyday life, people are constantly talking over and around each other, bodies are constantly moving, the camera is constantly moving, and there is so much information packed into every frame.

obviously, this is my bread and butter.

and the story is very good as well. watching neeta slowly sacrifice every part of herself for this family becomes a pretty brutal exploration of the cost of selflessness. everybody needs something from her. everybody takes something from her. and somehow her own life is always the thing that can wait.

I do wish i had been more emotionally involved though. for all the tragedy of what happens to her, i always felt at a distance from the film and from some of the family dynamics. certain relationships really worked, others considerably less.

but with filmmaking this formally exciting, i almost don’t care.

excellent outing.

letterboxd-review-1498529481.title: Charulata
letterboxd-review-1498529481.review:
I think what I continue to appreciate so much about ray is just how quietly he sets up his worlds. there’s never any urgency to explain the culture, the politics, the relationships or even what i’m supposed to be paying attention to. he just lets people live, and slowly you begin to understand everything surrounding them.

charaluta finding her own voice was the highlight of the film. it feels almost inevitable that she would discover this intellectual and creative side of herself through someone she also begins to fall in love with.
the writing, the attraction, the freedom she seems to find around amal.
I really liked all of that in theory, even if emotionally i don’t think the relationship itself ever affected me as much as i wanted it to.

my favorite moment is easily the swing sequence.  the movement, the close-ups, her face, the camera swinging with her. what they talk about. her creative turmoil…
a sequence directly inspired and influenced by jean renoir’s “a day in the country”. pure poetry.

ray also, with subtlety, successfully manages to explore without ever preaching everything happening culturally and politically around the story. the relationship these people have with british colonialism, the tension between tradition and modernity, all these little details about what india was going through at the time…

the husband was also a highlight in the performances. especially at the end. no simplistic depiction of masculinity. just people hurting each other, loving each other, failing each other and trying to understand what to do with all of it.

I guess the only thing keeping me at a slight distance is that i appreciated most of this more than i actually felt it.

which is strange because it follows a somewhat similar gradual structure to devi, but that film completely pulled me into its anxiety and tragedy. and I also found the imagery of that film overall more striking.
here, even though i thought almost everything was really well done, I was never quite as immersed in the characters or their relationships.

and maybe that’s why the moments that did connect with me, like the swing, stood out so much.

still, a really really solid film.

and with that, satyajit ray is done for now, on the indian cinema journey.

i’ll eventually come back to him, when the journey is done, to watch the big city and the hero. but so far, what an intro to this fabulous artist.

a profound humanist. a truth capturer. a master filmmaker!
he lived up to the hype, and deserves every ounce of praise.

but now, it is time for parallel cinema…

letterboxd-review-1497765980.title: Devi
letterboxd-review-1497765980.review:
the power of this film is in its silence.

it’s fascinating how quiet ray is with his filmmaking. the way people move. the way they look at each other. the way they listen. the patience he allows before someone says anything.

for the first 30 minutes, it feels like nothing is happening. and then, before you even realize it, the tension has slowly crescendoed into this suffocating anxiety.

because what makes devi so powerful is the way ray explores patriarchal oppression through the complete opposite of degradation.

doyamoyee isn’t treated as worthless. she’s worshipped.

she is elevated to the status of a goddess, but in doing so, she is still turned into an object. her identity, her desires, her agency, even her own understanding of herself are slowly taken away from her by the men around her. deification becomes another form of imprisonment.

and sharmila tagore is sublime. there’s something so haunting about her face as the pressure slowly consumes her. ray barely needs her to say anything.

but the film is just as interested in why these people need to believe in her in the first place. faith becomes a form of security in a world filled with uncertainty. and that need isn’t limited by class. the wealthy patriarch needs it just as much as the desperate people who eventually arrive looking for miracles.

ray just lets all of that pressure cook until tragedy becomes inevitable.

then it ends almost as abruptly as it began.

doyamoyee running into that field and slowly disappearing into the fog.

haunting.

powerful stuff.

letterboxd-review-1493713063.title: Apur Sansar
letterboxd-review-1493713063.review:
this f*cking guy can’t catch a break!

he cannot attach himself to anyone without them dying as soon as he does.

but alas, such is life…

because by the end of the trilogy, I don’t think these deaths are simply deaths anymore. each one represents the end of a period in apu’s life. something dies, something else is born, another storm comes, eventually the sun rises again, and on and on it spins.

there is no finish line until he dies.

and the world of apu might be the most complete expression of that idea.

what it loses in some of the innocence and magic of pather panchali, it gains through an incredible human story.

the entire premise of apu arriving at a wedding and somehow leaving with the bride is insane. but it also immediately throws you into cultural and societal traditions that i knew absolutely nothing about, and from that comes one of the most beautiful relationships in the trilogy.

the chemistry between apu and aparna is phenomenal.

you feel the awkwardness become curiosity, curiosity become affection, and affection become genuine passion. her close-ups are pure poetry. the little moments between them are so alive that you completely understand why losing her destroys him.

and for the first time, apu doesn’t simply continue, he runs.

he abandons his novel. abandons his child. disappears into the mountains and tries to escape life altogether.

and who hasn’t wanted to do that?

but eventually responsibility calls him back. because responsibility isn’t simply a burden. it’s also what gives life purpose.

his son gives him a reason to return to the world. his writing becomes inseparable from his own life. and after spending three films watching people disappear around him, apu ultimately chooses attachment again despite knowing exactly what attachment can cost.

that’s what makes the ending so wonderful.

the storms aren’t over. another one will come. then another sun will rise. two steps backward, one step forward, and then backward again. with hope always at the end if it. like in fellini films.

and while apu has grown across these three films, so has ray.

pather panchali felt almost entirely observational. ray simply captured life with an extraordinary humanist instinct. in aparajito, he began experimenting with subjectivity and using the form more deliberately to place us inside his characters.

here, he has completely mastered the craft.

the blocking is pristine. the camera movements are precise. the dolly push-ins, the compositions, the use of foreground and background with deep focus, wide shots becoming close ups. there are images of apu alone in nature that feel malickian. moments of blocking that echo kurosawa. compositions that echo bergman.

this is when the language of great filmmaking becomes universal. ray has absorbed the possibilities of the form and made them his own while never truly losing that observational quality that made pather panchali so special in the first place.

he started as a truth capturer. on top of that, he became a master filmmaker.

and that final sequence…

apu walking in a medium shot, while the child following him remains deep in the background of the frame.

once again, apu moves toward the unknown.

in pather panchali, he left with his family.
in aparajito, he walked away alone.
and now, finally, he walks forward carrying someone else.

what a meditation on love, death, attachment, grief, responsibility and the simple act of continuing to live despite all of it.

major work of art and a fantastic conclusion to the trilogy.

letterboxd-review-1490977718.title: Aparajito
letterboxd-review-1490977718.review:
This review may contain spoilers.

there’s a very good reason why it’s so fascinating watching apu evolve.

in pather panchali, he was almost the definition of innocence. a child whose imagination could be completely captured by a train, theatre, nature, the smallest things around him.

here, that innocence slowly becomes intellectual curiosity. he wants to learn. he wants to understand. he wants to leave. and with that comes the first real struggle between the life that made you and the life you want to make for yourself.

staying with your parents or moving forward on your own.

the past or the future.

and we always have the feeling that these two choices can’t coexist. and that’s not really true.

there’s a beautiful moment when apu comes home from school and deliberately misses his train back so he can spend one more day with his mother. he lies and tells her he missed it. he doesn’t particularly want to stay. he basically sleeps through the day. but at that age, he already understands that simply being there means something to her.

it’s an incredibly mature, selfless thing to do.

and then a couple moments later, faced with essentially the same choice, he stays in calcutta because he needs to study. and he never sees his mother again.

but ray never treats that decision as a mistake. that’s what makes it so interesting. apu was right to pursue his future. he was also right to stay with his mother that extra day. these things are allowed to contradict each other because that’s life.

by the end, death has become something apu understands in a completely different way. his sister. his father. now his mother. the people around him can love him, shape him and teach him, but ultimately they will come and go, and he has to continue on his own.

so when he refuses to remain behind and walks away at the end, there’s something profoundly different about that image from the ending of pather panchali.

once again, apu walks into the unknown. except this time he walks alone. sad, but determined.

and what is particularly fascinating is that while apu is evolving, satyajit ray is evolving alongside him.

not only did he have to deal with a bigger budget. so many locations and set pieces in this one.
but more importantly, there’s an evolution in the style:
pather panchali felt almost entirely observational. the camera captured life and allowed us to experience it. here, ray begins experimenting much more with subjectivity.

a voice becomes distant as the mother retreats into her own thoughts. she hears apu when he isn’t there. music suddenly takes on an almost thriller quality. the camera moves and sound changes not simply to observe reality, but to place us inside a character’s experience of it.

the naturalism is still there, but ray is beginning to manipulate it.

and that formal evolution fits quite well with a film constantly caught between tradition and modernity. the village and calcutta. parents and independence. childhood and adulthood.

i don’t think it’s quite as great as pather panchali. something of the magic of that film is missing here. maybe that’s inevitable because the innocence and wonder is incredibly difficult to capture a second time.

some moments also don’t carry quite the same emotional weight. the father’s death, for example, felt surprisingly abrupt. considering how important he was to this family in the first film (and even in the second film), there’s very little space afterward for grief. he dies and they never mention him again.

a few other moments didn’t hit as much, but all in all, an excellent sophomore feature.
