letterboxd-review-1488591157.title: Pather Panchali
letterboxd-review-1488591157.review:
there’s something that always astounds me about filmmakers like kiarostami, rossellini, and all the great film humanists.

they are so unapologetic about their culture, their people, their experiences. they don’t seem concerned with whether the rest of the world will understand them, whether a general audience will relate, or whether what they’re showing will be deemed worthy.

they just tell the truth the way they see it.

and somehow, by being as specific and honest as possible, they arrive at something completely universal.

Satyajit Ray (who had never held a camera before this) is no exception.

for the first 20 minutes of pather panchali, I felt like I had been dropped on another planet. knowing nothing of this culture, this village, these people, the way their lives work. I was trying to understand the engine of the world in front of me.

and you start thinking that maybe at the end of it you’ll admire it, but you won’t necessarily relate to it.

then slowly you realize this isn’t another planet. these aren’t aliens. these are fellow humans going through universal experiences.

because ray does it with such unflinching honesty that these incredibly small moments suddenly become gigantic moments of absolute poetry:

the insects moving across the water. durga standing in the rain. the old auntie looking back before leaving on her final journey. the reverse shot of the mother staring into the void. apu discovering theatre. the siblings cooking, fighting, running through fields.

and of course, the train…

the relationship between apu and durga has to be one of the greatest sibling relationships ever put to screen. and the moment when she promises him that when she gets better, they’ll go see the train again…

I’m not crying, you’re crying.

suddenly the train isn’t a train anymore. it’s that thing you shared with someone you loved. that thing that belonged to just the two of you. and after they’re gone, that thing will forever be a memory.

that’s the universal truth I’m talking about. and it’s unbelievably moving.

and so much of the film is about finding those tiny moments of happiness in a life otherwise defined by survival.

the struggle of survival.

durga steals. the mother does everything she can to keep the family together. the father wanted to be a playwright, but life doesn’t give him that luxury. he has to leave for months on end to come back with maybe just enough for food and clothes.

and that’s why food is constantly magnified in the film because survival is constantly present.

but the film also takes its time to magnify the little things: rain. a train. theatre. shooting arrows. making a crown.

and we see these little things through the lens of Apu. the lens of the child. the lens of innocence. watching his imagination become completely captured by the art he is discovering.

it’s also a story of women. and their sacrifices. the ones who shape our protagonist’s entire understanding of the world around him.

his mother. his sister. the old auntie…

through them he sees childhood, old age, suffering, sacrifice, joy, death and the passage of time. they teach him both how cruel life can be and where happiness can still be found within it.

and eventually, after generations of surviving and suffering, this family decides to break the chain and take their chances in the unknown. because for better or worst, remaining where you are, can no longer be the answer. what a final shot!

talking about shots…

the confidence is unbelievable. some of the blocking, some of the compositions, the faces (especially when they’re in close ups), the way scenes just flow into one another with instinctive editing.
some of the poetic images during the storm, especially those of the mother and sister, are extraordinary. the two shot of apu and durga when she promises they’ll see the train again is spectacular.

it’s all so elegant without ever calling attention to itself.

and learning that ray had actually illustrated an edition of pather panchali before making the film somehow makes perfect sense. you can feel someone who had already been living with these images, thinking visually about this world, long before he ever had the opportunity to put a camera in front of it.

i started this film feeling like i was looking into a world i knew absolutely nothing about.

i ended it crying over a train.

i guess that’s the whole point.

indian cinema journey is starting a little too strong.

letterboxd-review-1487385055.title: I Want Your Sex
letterboxd-review-1487385055.review:
there’s something important about reminding younger generations that it’s okay to be horny. actually, it’s a duty to be horny!
sex is cool. sex is fun. sex is life. it’s the reason you’re here. and sometimes it’s overrated. but other times it’s pretty awesome. there should be no shame around it.

so at a time when people are having less sex than ever, i found it interesting to have a film actually confront that shame and try to understand why our relationship with sex has become what it is.

but araki also doesn’t blindly celebrate everything that comes with it. once the film gets into BDSM, manipulation and consent, it becomes genuinely interesting morally. where are the limits. how easily can those lines become blurred. how far can you truly push someone.

I appreciate what the film tackles on.

it’s not a great movie by any means, and I’ll probably forget it very soon, but I’m glad it exists.

letterboxd-review-1484217069.title: Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie
letterboxd-review-1484217069.review:
not nearly as laugh out loud funny throughout as the first 15 minutes had me thinking it would be.

however I was so in awe of the craft. it’s kind of insane.

you genuinely never know what is real and what isn’t. you don’t know if the people in the background are extras or actual people who have no idea they’re being filmed. you don’t know what they had permission to do and what they just did off the cuff.

and then something so insane happens that you think, well, obviously this had to be planned.

but was it?

there’s something almost anxiety-inducing about never knowing.

it feels like this strange collision between borat, where so much of the comedy comes from interacting with an unsuspecting real world, and incredibly meticulous, strategically planned filmmaking. and the way it constantly blurs that line is something i don’t think i’ve ever quite seen done like this before.

and the execution is flawless.

I mean, the attention to detail. every camera, every bit of grain, every glitch, the type of handheld, even the billboards from 2008… all impeccably authentic.

the story itself is good too. simple, heartfelt, fun. however I was never really pushed over the edge emotionally.

it was a joyful time. and what a feat in filmmaking!

and yes, better than the odyssey.

letterboxd-review-1456409676.title: The End of Oak Street
letterboxd-review-1456409676.review:
believe it or not, I was excusing a lot of the film’s shortcomings for the better part of the first 30-40 minutes.

the god-awful dialogue. the god-awful exposition. the terrible acting from the kids.

because I could see what it was trying to do. and what it was trying to do was a twilight zone episode. what it was trying to do was to bring us back to the golden age of amblin. the masterpieces of spielberg and tobe hooper.
there was a semblance of that magic there. and because of that, I was willing to go along and give it the benefit of the doubt.

I also liked that it took its time before the dinosaurs appeared. they took the right amount of time to establish the family and their dynamic but the problem was that it executed all of it so terribly. the conflict between mcgregor and hathaway was not believable, what the kids said was not natural. compare those kids performances to the kids in jurassic park for a second. night and day.

still, I was with it.

the dinosaurs arrive, the flashing lights work (reminiscent of poltergeist), the designs are solid, the cgi is mostly good, and I loved that they had hair and feathers (finally realistic). overall, the world was decently established.

then the rollercoaster starts and somehow everything gets worse.
the acting gets worse. the writing gets worse. the filmmaking gets worse…

there’s this bizarre visual language in the beginning with split diopters being used constantly in very odd places, sometimes cutting directly from a split-diopter shot to another split diopters shot and then back to a completely normal shot for no apparent reason.
there’s a scene where everyone is sitting around in a circle and it just keeps doing this over and over again. it’s unclear what the intention was. it’s not expressive, or properly stylistic. it’s just jarring.

and then you realize there really isn’t a story to root for because the emotional anchor (ewan and anne) is a mess.
the film overstays its welcome by at least an hour.
(this probably should have been the length of a twilight zone episode)

then the film can never decide how grounded it wants to be.
it spends so much time early on trying to create a believable world, and then suddenly starts picking and choosing when realism matters.

a t-rex does not sneak up behind you.
this is a 20,000 pound animal. you’d hear it and the ground would shake. but they don’t hear it for “comedic effect” but even that doesn’t work.

then you have moments like the t-rex going after hathaway and somehow being stopped by a couple of home pillars that an animal of that size would obviously destroy.
and normally i wouldn’t even care about things like that, but when a film establishes a certain level of groundedness and then abandons it whenever it needs a joke or an action beat, you stop knowing what the rules are, and therefore stop suspending your disbelief.

the emotional scenes have the same problem.

mcgregor and hathaway’s relationship is so badly written and so underdeveloped that none of it lands. there’s a moment where they’re trapped together in the car thinking they’re about to die, and for maybe a second you think there could actually be something there.

and then the scene ends before it has time to breathe. before it has time to say anything. before you have time to feel anything.
not that the character development was really there to begin with, but I’m just saying.

and then there’s the dumbass subplots.

my god.

the little boy being chased down and punched because he broke someone’s brother’s arm could have been removed entirely in the edit and absolutely nothing would change. i genuinely can’t believe those scenes survived into the final cut.

the subplot with the girl is slightly less terrible, but still adds almost nothing.
and the longer the film goes, the more convoluted it becomes until eventually it just collapses into absolute nothingness.

the resolution is rushed, anticlimactic and completely underwhelming.

i’m still giving it a couple of stars because of those first 30-40 minutes, where I did feel a little bit of that old amblin magic.

it’s as bad as it follows.

and yes, much worse than the odyssey.

letterboxd-review-1452314747.title: The Hidden
letterboxd-review-1452314747.review:
my research is almost at an end. 2 more films to go. and this one was the closest one to what I’m working on in terms of premise.

it wasn’t great but it was fun kitsch.

a bit of sci-fi, a bit of crime, some relatable and funny banter between the two leads, and enough cool moments to keep it moving.

unfortunately we stay a little too emotionally distant from kyle maclachlan’s character. we’re told what happened to him, but we never really feel his plight. and i would’ve liked the film to dig a little deeper into the villain’s motivation. it’s never really clear.

but honestly, this has heart, and knows exactly what kind of movie it attempts to be.

as good as the odyssey.

letterboxd-review-1450580270.title: It Follows
letterboxd-review-1450580270.review:
2 stars is generous.

there’s no way anyone genuinely likes this.

beyond the cool premise, a very effective opening sequence, and a pretty solid performance from our protagonist, there is nothing to work with.

it’s not scary. it’s not dreadful. it’s not insightful. it’s not atmospheric.

and a big reason for that is that the writing is ridiculous and, outside of the main performance, nobody knows how to act.
every interaction is artificial. every emotional beat plays like people pretending to be in a movie instead of actual human beings reacting to what is happening.

the characters are barely characters. everyone is one note. there is no development. even the protagonist is given nothing beyond being the person this thing is happening to.

so there’s 0 reason to care.

the filmmaking is fine. it does the job. but even that doesn’t really stand out. the score is probably the best part of the movie, but even then, that’s not saying much.

and you can clearly see that the film wants to be less about plot and more about this constant eery feeling that something is coming. something is creeping behind you. almost attempting to create a feeling of claustrophobia as this thing that is following, it can never truly be escaped.

and it’s executed dreadfully.

there are no real surprises. almost everything goes exactly where you think it’s going to go. and even moments that are supposed to be intense become ridiculous because of the performances.

the girl gets shot in the leg and barely looks hurt.

the guy constantly trying to get into the protagonist’s pants is unbelievably cringey.

this is just nothing pretending to be something.
and it could’ve been an email.

letterboxd-review-1432034231.title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day
letterboxd-review-1432034231.review:
This review may contain spoilers.

contrary to what some of you may think, i don’t want to be right all the time (or most of the time). I want to be proven wrong. I want early reactions to be trustworthy. i want that 4.1 average to actually be somewhat accurate. believe it or not, i really do.

but alas… here we go again.

and before someone says I went in biased, I didn’t.  I am 95% of the time immune to biases. I joke about these things online, sure. but the second the lights go down and the projector turns on, my mind goes blank. I’ve been pleasantly surprised by plenty of films I thought I was going to hate. and funnily enough, for the first 20 minutes of this, I was in.

unfortunately after that, as much as I tried, the quality spoke for itself.

first things first. no, this isn’t a good movie. but more than that, it’s a highly forgettable movie. it’s barely a good spider-man movie.
and when it ended I actually found myself slightly nostalgic for the raimi trilogy (yes, even spider-man 3)
we’re so far removed from that level of filmmaking and storytelling that i don’t think we appreciate enough what we had.

now, some of you are going to ask how i can rate this lower than homecoming, no way home, or far from home.
the truth is, I don’t actually think those films are better. I actually believe that if I were to rewatch them (I won’t), i’d most likely rate then lower than bnd (except for maybe no way home).

the difference is context.

those tom holland spidey films came out during the absolute peak of the MCU. we weren’t just judging them as individual films. we were judging them as chapters in something much bigger. there was a level of excitement and goodwill surrounding marvel that inevitably elevated the experience.

that time is gone. we have now entered the dark ages of MCU slop. and so post endgame, we’re judging these films on their own.

and when brand new day has to stand on its own…

do I really have to go through everything that doesn’t work... I’d rather talk to you about the one thing that did work. but sure, I’ll rapidly go through the glaring flaws.

the writing is painfully predictable. the emotional moments are forced rather than earned (especially the MJ stuff. what wasted potential).
every major plot point goes exactly where you think it’s gonna go. it lacks as much creativity in the story as it does in the uninspired camera work.

the structure and pacing are also a mess.
the hulk fight and that whole sequence plays like a third act climax. except it isn’t. so the film peaks too early and never really recovers. everything that follows feels smaller, and the momentum disappears.

jean grey is another example of wasted potential. she’s barely developed. her motivations, her backstory… everything is reduced to its simplest possible version. we’re constantly being told to care instead of actually being given reasons to.

and so all in all, the emotional core never exists. (and the MCU used to craft incredible emotional cores)

there is, however, one thing i genuinely loved:

the punisher.

more specifically, the dynamic between bernthal and holland. that worked.
bernthal is fantastic. their banter is funny, their chemistry feels natural, and that is the only time I had a genuine smile on my face.

honestly, if this had just been a buddy comedy between the two, it would’ve probably been a masterpiece.

that’s also what’s a little frustrating. there are glimpses of a much better film buried in here.
they’re just buried beneath a screenplay that constantly settles for the easiest, safest, most obvious choice.

is this the worst tom holland spider-man? maybe. who knows.

but in no way home’s defense, for all of its cameo-driven fan service and its glaring plot holes, it at least had genuine emotion. it had actual ideas. the green goblin alone in that film carried more weight than anything in brand new day.

anyways, I’ve already forgotten about this film. I upheld my duty, that’s all that matters.

hopefully next time, I’ll be wrong. 🤞

letterboxd-review-1430006265.title: The Third Man
letterboxd-review-1430006265.review:
much like zodiac. I was not immersed the first time around, found it slow and uninteresting.
this time, fully immersed and it flew by like a breeze.

so beyond the impeccable craft, the dutch angles, the innovative work of shadows, the performances, and the incredible use of a bombed out post war vienna that feels like one of the greatest noir settings ever put on screen, I realized that beyond the mystery, this is a thorough deconstruction of american idealism.

joseph cotten’s character, like a good self centered american, walks into this world believing morality is simple. there are good people, and bad people, and doing the right thing will naturally lead to the right outcome. but every encounter slowly chips away at that certainty. until he’s forced to confront a world that’s infinitely more morally complex than he could’ve ever conceived of.

that’s what stayed with me the most.

in the end, doing the right thing doesn’t reward him. if anything, it leaves him more alone than he’s ever been. the film rejects the comforting idea that morality is transactional or that virtue guarantees happiness. life is way more complex than that. and this film makes sure you understand that.

this is what makes that last shot so haunting!

the one note I have is that Harry Lime feels a little caricatural after his iconic entrance. and he doesn’t have enough screen time which makes the climax feel a tad too abrupt.

nevertheless, a brilliant film.

letterboxd-review-1423931381.title: Zodiac
letterboxd-review-1423931381.review:
it’s funny how when you’re not immersed in the first 20 minutes of a film, it’s incredibly easy to get lost in the plot and lose all type of care for it. especially with procedural films like this.
so many characters, so many names, so many locations, so much dialogue, and if you don’t care about the investigation itself, all you’re left with is information. and information is boring.

that’s exactly what happened the first time i watched zodiac. I admired the craft but I couldn’t wait for it to be over.

this time, i was immersed immediately. and those issues disappeared.
but the big difference that happened with this viewing experience, was that I didn’t see the film as an investigation, but as an exploration of desperation. of obsession. of people who become so consumed by justice that they’re willing to lose absolutely everything in pursuit of it. their family. their health. their sanity. and it does all that while critiquing the american justice system that keeps working against them every step of the way.

everybody loses. and that’s why this third act works so well.

the tension is incredible because fincher hides it so well. the dread slowly crescendos over nearly three hours until you’re carrying the same exhaustion as the characters themselves. you never see it coming.

another thing i appreciated a lot this time around was the direction of the secondary performances. with this many characters, you won’t remember everybody’s name and fincher knows that. so he makes sure you remember everybody through attitude instead. the way they walk. the way they talk. the way they eat.
even if someone only has five minutes of screen time, they feel completely lived in. and that does so much for the immersion.

craft is impeccable but the only thing holding it back is a fundamental emotional layer.

for example, memories of murder explores many of these same ideas, executes them perfectly, while also delivering an emotional payoff that make it one of the best of the genre.

fight club and se7en also have that same emotional depth underneath their craft.
zodiac is missing that. it’s not the best fincher, but I can confidently say it’s as brilliant as the social network.

letterboxd-review-1408685940.title: The Odyssey
letterboxd-review-1408685940.review:
This review may contain spoilers.

there’s a reason early reviews either need to be completely ignored. or taken with a massive grain of salt.
whether it’s people calling something a masterpiece or the worst film ever made, the reality usually lies somewhere in between. the odyssey is no exception. there’s a lot to admire here, and there’s a lot that doesn’t work. let’s get into it.

first, the good news. all of the worries of the trailer. all of the “historical inaccuracies” (costumes, ship design, casting, geography etc..) otherwise known very famously as the “zoel issues” are a complete non issue.
the costumes are great and feel authentic (that’s why one must never look at screen grabs from google images, and always look at things within their proper context, with the proper lighting). the production design is great as well. the locations are real. the sets feel tangible. everything feels lived in.
under any other director, this would’ve been a cgi slop fest, but nolan’s commitment to practical filmmaking is once again the film’s greatest strength.

the writing, unfortunately, is where everything starts to fall apart. (this is not an issue with the particularly translation nolan chose to adapt, which I actually found quite fascinating. it’s how he executed on it)

the opening is overloaded with exposition, the dialogue swings wildly between genuinely compelling and painfully theatrical, at the cost of feeling redundant (hey, have you heard of Zeus’ law? they don’t mention it enough in the film)
and because every character is underdeveloped, because none of them are given enough room to become actual people, it makes a lot of sense that some of the delivery would feel flat or hollow.

yes, homer’s characters are archetypal, but I still cared more about them on the page than i did on the screen. because nolan gives us just enough information to understand who these people are, but almost never enough time to actually care about them.

that’s what keeps happening throughout the film.

circe is cool. calypso is lovely. athena is a breath of fresh air. the cyclop is beautifully designed. scylla is effectively economical in how she’s portrayed. even the giants look great. and the underworld sequence is probably one of my favorites.

but every sequence arrives, and then disappears just as quickly, before it has time to emotionally settle. the same is true of the human moments. we never really get to properly sit with odysseus and his family, or odysseus and his crew (and I’m not talking about being visually with them during the storm) I’m saying that we never actually explore or fully understand their camaraderie, their friendships, or what each loss actually means to the people left behind.
the film rarely lingers long enough on these moments for any of them to become truly immersive or memorable.

this is where I think the comparison with dunkirk becomes interesting.
dunkirk is also an emotionally restrained film built largely on mood, texture and experience. but dunkirk never promises you an emotional anchor. this does.
the opening immediately establishes odysseus, his wife and his son. the music tells you this family is going to be the emotional center of the film. everything points toward that reunion. you are supposed to feel emotionally invested in his journey and feeling the dread that he may never come back home.
so as opposed to dunkirk, the film does have the ambition to be emotional. but unfortunately never really delivers on that promise.

another thing i kept hearing before watching was how terrifying some of the monster sequences supposedly were. especially the cyclop sequence.
they aren’t.
they’re well crafted. beautifully designed. but I never once felt genuine fear, dread or horror. and i think that comes back to the exact same issue we’re having.
horror requires patience. tension requires scenes to breathe. and as we’ve established, this film is constantly moving from one event to the next without any proper payoff.

the cinematography is similarly inconsistent.

sometimes it’s absolutely gorgeous, motivated, and artful. particularly when we’re onboard the ships experiencing the voyage almost through odysseus’ eyes. that’s where the handheld work really shines.
being physically present with these characters, surrounded by real landscapes, is where the film is visually at its strongest.
other times, the camera moves feel random and lazy, especially during the jason bourne fight sequence at the end.

the score follows a similar pattern.

whenever it’s focused on the family, it’s wonderful. simple melodies that immediately communicate warmth, longing and intimacy.
during much of the action, though, it falls back on fairly generic percussion that simply accelerates alongside the editing without adding any emotional texture. i’d heard people calling this ludwig göransson’s masterpiece. it’s far from it.
oppenheimer wins that conversation by a mile.

now unto the performances…
I’m afraid to say matt damon is still… matt damon. and he’s still… just there. I kept hearing about his special and transformative performance. I never saw it.
he gives a perfectly good matt damon performance.
I just don’t think he possesses the gravitas the character of odysseus actually requires.

anne hathaway is excellent and easily gives the strongest performance in the film.

tom holland actually surprised me. i wouldn’t call it extraordinary, but he absolutely holds his own and makes the most of the material he’s given.

robert pattinson, unfortunately, didn’t convince me at all. perhaps it’s partly because the character is written as a one-note antagonist, but the performance often drifted into caricature.

zendaya and eliott page were great (especially in the underworld)

everyone else ranges somewhere between good, very good, and forgettable.

thematically, the film touches on war, imperialism, identity, guilt and the gradual loss of self. and for the most part it’s all there, but the anti-war messaging itself never goes much beyond mere ideas we’ve seen explored many times before and often with far greater depth.

and now here’s the contradiction. the very thing that kept me emotionally distant is also ironically one of the things i admired the most: the editing and structure.

yes, I found it jarring and frustrating. as I said, we constantly jump from one event to another without much transition or reflection. however, it also does something I’ve never really seen before.

the film is edited like its source material. every scene feels like a poetic verse and every shot feels like a stanza.
it’s nolan translating not just the story of an epic poem but its rhythm and structure into a fascinating cinematic language. an exploration of form and texture. a formidable exercise in style, executed quasi flawlessly.

so all in all, this isn’t a masterpiece. far from it. it doesn’t come remotely close to oppenheimer, interstellar, or even any of nolan’s strongest film.
but also here’s the thing, the odyssey is in many ways, an impossible work to adapt. arguably unfilmable. so the fact that nolan did so, with this level of creativity, originality, dedication to the sheer craft of filmmaking while maintaining the absolute epicness of it all, is something I can’t help but celebrate and applaud. and it’s enough for me to recommend the odyssey.

PS: the dune 3 clip that was shown before the movie started, was out of this world!

PSS: the overt glaze or overt hate for any new big release is an actual issue in film discourse today (but that’s a problem we’ll have to tackle at another time)

letterboxd-review-1367558881.title: Flathead
letterboxd-review-1367558881.review:
flathead is quite impressive. especially for a first short film.

the camera work is very confident. intentional, and surprisingly mature.
handheld filmmaking is often used in low budget shorts as a crutch, a way to hide limitations, and more often than not it ends up being terrible. unmotivated, ugly, and cheap.

here, it feels completely deliberate.
every movement, every whip pan, every reframing feels considered. even more impressive is how precise the framing remains despite the camera constantly moving.
Brayden showcases a real understanding of composition as well as a keen eye for framing.
very reminiscent of succession and the bear’s visual language.

the performances are good, some better than others, and the central conflict has potential. I wonder what it would look like as a web series.
my main criticism is that the narrative doesn’t dig deep enough. the characters are interesting, but not fully explored. at the end i wasn’t as emotionally invested as i wanted to be. the piece works as a proof of concept, but i was left wanting more than the format was able to provide.

overall, this is better than most first short films i’ve seen. a lot of talent on display, particularly behind the camera, and cinema council can certainly be proud. I’m excited to see what he does next.

I implore all of you to go watch Flathead on @cinemacouncil’s youtube.

letterboxd-review-1546545541.title: The Lunchbox
letterboxd-review-1546545541.review:
lovely, lovely film. such a quietness to it all, a restraint in the storytelling. the idea of a home cooked meal made with care and passion, connecting two people who would otherwise never have met is wonderful.

and it also feels so personal, so culturally specific. the whole system of lunchboxes being prepared by your spouse at home and delivered to their husband at work is something completely foreign to us westerners. I was actually a little confused at first, but the film introduces us to this world very naturally that you quickly get to understand how it all works, how it’s simply part of these people’s everyday lives.

and within those daily routines, there’s this overwhelming sense of monotony, loneliness, and more importantly grief. through this epistolary relationship, we slowly discover not only the pain these two people carry, but also that of so many others around them.

i did however find it a little uneven emotionally. some moments genuinely moved me (thanks to the writing and the brilliantly subdued performance of khan), while others didn’t resonate nearly as much. I liked the supporting character, very funny in the beginning which then became a very nice addition to the character of khan, even if he didn’t necessarily leave a lasting impression.

as for the filmmaking, there are two things that stood out. on the one hand, i loved the shot choices. there’s an almost constant use of frames within frames, very few cuts, and a camera that often keeps its distance from the characters, simply observing them. there’s a patience to that approach that works perfectly with the tone of the film.

on the other hand however, I didn’t love the cinematography itself, especially the overexposed lighting. some shots have this strange, almost videoish quality that doesn’t feel cinematic at all, even though the film seems to be striving for a cinematic image. i’m not entirely sure what the intention was there, or whether it was intentional at all, but i found it slightly jarring.

all in all, a really solid debut, quite a strong ending, and a wonderful exploration on alienation.
